newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Two consortia take shape in race to bid for CVRD.
newsitem.headline: Two consortia take shape in race to bid for CVRD.

text.p: Two major groups are taking shape to bid for state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) when it is partialy privatised on April 29.

A strategic 45 percent block of voting shares in CVRD is being sold off at a base price of three billion reais ($2.83 billion). The emerging consortia are the result of a split last week between Brazilian metals, cement and pulp group Votorantim and the country's largest steelmaker, Companhia Siderurgica Nacional (CSN).

"It looks like Votorantim wants to form a block in which it holds a leading role. If that is the case, then we are not interested," said Maria Silvia Bastos Marques, director of CSN's corporate sector.
"The precondition for our consortium is a power equilibrium, or shared control. We are not going to join a consortium in which we have no say."

Since the split, Votorantim President Antonio Ermirio de Moraes has spoken to the media about his plans to join Japanese investors and another foreign group, believed to be South Africa's Anglo American Corp.
"We are talking to Nippon Steel, one of CVRD's biggest iron ore clients, which would join us representing other Japanese buyers," Moraes told Jornal do Brasil.

"Apart from them, we have other important partners: CVRD employees, who can buy up to 4.5 percent (of CVRD); pension funds who already hold 15 percent of the company; Banco Safra; and a foreign group."
Meanwhile, CSN is in an advanced stage of talks with Brazil's biggest retail bank, Bradesco, and South African mining firm Gencor Ltd.

"We are talking to pension funds, CVRD's employees, Gencor, Bradesco and other potential partners, mainly national ones," Marques said. "What CSN would prefer is a shared control consortium where you have a national majority preferably."
Moraes told reporters he was surprised that CSN and Bradesco broke ranks with Votorantim, which would have allowed CVRD to remain largely under Brazilian control.
"We have to do everything to keep the center of decisions on CVRD in Brazil," Moraes told Veja magazine. "Iron ore is an important wealth and its ours."

The joint Votorantim/CSN consortium was also the government's preferred future owner of CVRD due to its nationalist credentials, which would have staved off criticism that a large part of Brazil's mineral wealth was being handed to foreigners.
